[Edit 16 Aug 2025]: I decided to jump in and figure out how to modify the Trumpeter kit on my own. For anyone who is interested, I will post my progress in this thread.

I just got my Trumpeter 1:350 USS Intrepid, with the goal of converting it to the USS Hornet in her post SCB-27A and SCB-125 configuration. This would be as she was on my Dad’s first deployment on her in 1959. My good friends at the USS Hornet museum have been very helpful in providing photos of the primary differences, which include the flight deck shape, the catapult locations, the forward elevator shape, the #3 elevator location, and the mast configuration. There may be other smaller differences, but these are the noticeable ones (I believe) for 1:350 scale. My biggest challenge is the flight deck, where there are major differences, and I am not convinced that trying to modify it is the best approach, which is why I’m considering building a flight deck from scratch in the proper configuration. I have put the correct configuration into Inkscape, so I have a vector rendering that includes the location for the island, the correct elevator sizes and locations, and the correct catapult locations and sizes. Has anyone undertaken a project like this? It would also be ideal to find pre-scribed styrene or wood with the proper dimensions, as the flight deck on Hornet was 100% wood in 1959. Is it possible to get a flight deck of this size (almost 30") 3D printed?

I had to break down the differences between my target configuration and the kit across a couple of dimensions. First, I started with getting the correct configuration of the Hornet for this era. As you might expect, most of the photos and data online are for the Apollo 11 recovery configuration, which has some subtle but noticeable differences from the 1959 Westpac configuration.

The 1959 configuration of the Hornet is somewhat ephemeral. To the best of my knowledge, this configuration only lasted a couple of years, with obvious visual changes being the mast and the various antennas, the SPN-8 vs. the SPN-35 for radar-controlled approaches, and the general painting and appearance of the flight deck. Also, each island structure in the post-SCB Essexes has subtle differences. Here, I chose to get the Model Monkey Hornet island, which will be very close to what I need, even though it’s the 1969 Apollo 11 configuration.

Fortunately, I have my Dad’s cruisebook with tons of pictures from that cruise. This proved to be indispensable. My other secret weapon was the ship herself. I lived in the Bay Area for a few years and was lucky enough to serve as a docent on the Hornet. The docents are very knowledgeable and helpful and I’ve been able to correspond with them to check on various aspects of the ship’s layout that can help me get the right configuration. I highly recommend a visit to the ship if you’re ever in the area.

Knowing now the nuances of the 1959 Hornet, I compared the correct configuration to theTrumpeter kit. That’s when I realized the magnitude of this undertaking.

The most obvious differences from this perspective are the shape and size of the #1 elevator and the location of the #3 (aft stbd) elevator. The catapults are also very different in size and location (Intrepid had newer steam catapults vs. Hornet’s hydraulic cats. The Intrepid also had much of its original deck planking covered with a thick non-skid coating that obscured the planking below it. The 1959 Hornet was almost completely showing the planked flight deck. Here’s what you get when you overlay the outline of the Hornet’s flight deck with that of the Intrepid:

Anthony_Newpower
Aug 2025

The Trumpeter kit’s flight deck has a nice level of detail, but given the nature of the lack of planking in key areas, the size and shape of the #1 elevator, and the location of the #3 elevator, I decided that I needed to build my own flight deck to get the details and shape right. I considered 3 main options:

  1. Laser cut basswood. This would probably return a pretty good result, provided the laser kern was fine enough to capture the planking details and the aircraft tiedowns. I opted against this option, since the software needed to make this was different that what I had been using and my learning curve on that software was already steep enough. I have been using Inkscape to render the 2D drawings of the flight deck, along with making the decals I will need. I will talk about that more in a follow-up post.
  2. I considered just getting a piece of ABS cut to the right size and shape for my flight deck, but the lack of planking and tiedown detail meant this could only really serve as a base to laminate a thin, detailed layer on top. I considered a printed deck to put on top, either with very thin wood or just paper itself. The 2D nature of this, even at 1:350 scale, put me off.
  3. 3D printing. This is what I’m going with, and I purchased a 3D printer (Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra) to experiment with this process. I liked the level of detail it could offer and there’s lots of free software you can use to make the printable files.

I’ve been reconsidering my flight deck options, but have commissioned a 3D print of the flight deck. Given the size of the flight deck, I had to break it up into 4 pieces for printing. Fortunately, the Hornet has expansion joints that run across the flight deck, making for convenient points to split the deck. I have not given up on laser cutting basswood, either. I think that if the engraving of the planks was done right, this could turn out really well.

The 3D printing experience for me has been very good. In addition to learning Inkscape for the flight deck, I have used Blender to design my 3D shapes, and Lychee to slice them and make them ready for printing. Results have been very good for me so far. I printed the mast of the 1959 Hornet in 3D as a single unit. So much easier than fiddling with each individual part. I will still need to add railings and the radars, but I’m super happy with how the mast turned out:

Thanks for the kind words, mrb865. I’ll definitely keep the updates coming! Today, I decided to make sure once and for all that I had #3 elevator aligned with the flight deck and the hangar deck bulkheads. Since I had to cut those parts and graft the hangar deck opening for the elevator further forward, I could not take advantage of the locating pins for the elevator guides (parts F6 and F7). I cut those pins off, along with the three triangular supports on each guide near the bottom. On Hornet, these guides attach directly to the sponsons, the forward one I 3D printed and the after sponson is the crane sponson, so it’s mainly a matter of moving that sponson to be flush with the guide, but getting those parts flush is not that easy. What I decided to do was to mount the elevator guide structure (part F5) to the elevator, so that I could insert it into the guides, which would guarantee they are correctly spaced. Once I had the elevator in the guides, I attached them to the the bulkhead structure, leaving the elevator in place as the glue set. Now, I can install the sponsons and when the time comes to mate the bulkhead and the guides together with the sponsons, everything should be perfectly spaced.

Anthony_Newpower
Nov 2025

I also changed my strategy on the interior hangar bay bulkheads. Originally, I was trying to make them thicker and stiffer, but that just seemed to exacerbate warping, despite many efforts on my part to straighten them. Therefore, I’m going to go with relatively thin (1.5mm) bulkheads that I can glue to the external bulkheads and just have them conform by force. These are a bit more fragile, so cutting them from their supports is a more delicate operation–I broke 1 bulkhead in half even before curing, and another chipped at a thin point. I may just re-print them with a few minor adjustments.

Anthony_Newpower
Apr 23

Well, I’ve hit another engineering challenge. The Intrepid has a somewhat different system for the #2 elevator tracks than does the Hornet. And since this is on the starboard side, and Hornet is moored port side to, it’s difficult to get good pictures and measurements of the elevator. Here’s a picture I took on my most recent visit, and knowing full well that I needed to make these modifications. I did not think it would be as challenging as it’s turning out to be. Note that the tracks for the elevator angle inward, approximately 5 degrees. This is meant to account for the fact that, at flight deck level, there’s a considerable amount of deck overhang to the superstructure, what I estimate to be around 5mm in 1:350. At the hangar deck level, this drops by about half, due to fact that the tracks angle inward as the elevator goes down. I did not account for this when I had the flight deck printed, so I am planning on printing a plug for the flight deck to close this gap. I will have to do the same at the hangar deck level. I am also considering moving the truss inward by a few mm to see what that does. It will probably look better if I don’t have to graft onto the flight deck. Since I plan on posing the elevator at the hangar deck, I could also just ignore the gap at the top, since a casual observer won’t be able to tell anything is wrong. The nuclear option would be to have the deck re-printed, but I am not seriously considering that…yet…

I had to design and print new superstructure aft of the elevator, since the kit piece is very different. That seemed to have worked ok, but I won’t know for sure until I do another test print and try to join it up to the rest of the superstructure. By the time I’m done, I will probably have replaced 75% of the superstructure on the port side, when originally, I thought I’d probably have nothing to replace there…

For comparison, I have included two screenshots of Intrepid’s elevator, and you can see that the track supports are totally different. They also appear to be almost straight up and down, moving without an angle on the tracks.

I’m doing a little bit of work on the Model Monkey island. I will probably treat it as a separate model and build it fully, paint it and have it ready to install on the flight deck as a complete unit. This should make doing the rigging, installing antennas, railings, etc. a bit easier. The Model Monkey island is excellent, but it is circa 1969, 10 years after my era, and there were some changes, most notably the SPN-6 approach radar from the 1959 cruise was replaced with the SPN-35. Both were mounted on the aft end of the island, but the SPN-35 sits inside a much larger domed housing than the SPN-6. So I cut off the SPN-35 housing and designed a smaller one that I will 3D print. Model Monkey also provides the SPN-6 in their catalog, so I purchased and will use that on my mount. There was also a semi-circular indent on the deck where the SPN-35 was mounted, so I trimmed off a bit of the original mount and fitted it into that recess. With some CA and accelerator, and a lot of sanding, I’ve got it ready to take the new mount. Patience is key when sawing the resin, as it is fully cured and more brittle as a result. I have the island cleaned up mostly, but have a little bit of filler sanding to do, then I’ll fit the new mount. The first photo shows the SPN-6, and the second the SPN-35. You can see how much bigger the -35 is.

Anthony_Newpower
Jul 4

Happy 4th and 250th to everyone! Looks like it was quite a show in NYC today; here in Colorado, we’re celebrating, but cautiously due to the fire danger. So, I’ve been doing more research today, and I learned something important. In my previous post, I mentioned doing the sponsons for the Hornet, as they differed from the Intrepid. Well, after looking at my 1959 cruise book, I noticed something, namely, that there were no visible sponsons on the starboard side, but instead it appeared that there were small platforms to assist with the UNREPs. This got me looking to confirm the layout and I went online to the great navsite.de page to consult the 1958 and 1957 Hornet Cruise Books. Lo and behold, I finally found what I was looking for in this great shot from the 1957 Cruise Book. Thank you, Supply Department. It’s clear in this shot that there were no sponsons at the deck level, but there is in fact a sponson of sorts under the island, just forward of the escalator enclosure. The 1957 cruise book has an awesome UNREP section, and I was able to get pictures of this command and control sponson from all angles. Knowing the rate of change and evolution of the Essex class during this time, just because it was there in 1957 did not mean it would be there in 1959. I did find compelling enough evidence of its presence in 1959 from that cruise book in a bow-on shot. So, I made reasonable guesstimates of the size of the sponson and am doing a test print now. I will also be removing the deck-level sponsons and instead will fit small platforms where the sponsons would be installed later, most likely during the 1961 refit at Puget Sound NSY. I have enjoyed the detective work to get this configuration right. There does not seem to be a definitive source for this configuration, so it’s up to me to create it!

For those who have read this thread, you probably know that I’d prefer 100% accuracy, but I’ll make do this time!

Anthony_Newpower
Jul 16

Also, while starting to do more research on the island itself, I discovered a pretty major discrepancy between the Model Monkey Hornet island and how the island was configured in 1959. The Model Monkey island is for the Apollo 11 recovery era–1969–and it turns out there were some noticeable changes there, besides the SPN-6 being replaced by the SPN-35. And though I was able to make that change, there is a considerably more tricky difference on the forward portion of the tallest section of the island–namely, a large rectangular box that sits on that face for the 1969 version, but is not present in 1959. Given the prominence of this piece and the trickiness of trying to remove the box, I looked at the other Model Monkey offerings and determined that the USS Yorktown island for 1955-1960 is, as far as I can tell, a very accurate rendering for the Hornet in 1959, which makes sense. And, bonus, it comes with the SPN-6 already integrated, though it is missing the platform for the SPS-8 height finding radar that is present on the Hornet island. Not to worry, I designed and printed my own platform, along with the mast for the SPS-29 radar on the starboard side of the island. The kit has this in PE, but it will look 2D on the ship, so I opted for printing it as well. It’s a bit delicate, but I feel I should be able to get it in place without too much fiddling. I tried to print the railing around the radar antenna platform, but it was a bit too fine for my printer to replicate.

Another lesson learned today, and fortunately before I started painting the flight deck. It turned out that in the SCB-125 refit, a steel plate was installed in the impact area around the arresting cables, presumably to better handle the larger aircraft and higher speeds you would see on the angled deck. Although I had primed the flight deck, mercifully, I did not paint it. I turned to my sheet styrene supplies and found some .13mm paper thin styrene. I was able to scale the sheet from my blueprints and cut it to size. I will now attach with CA after I remove some of the primer from the mating surface. Very happy I found this before painting, since it will be very noticeable!

So I’m starting to think about the hangar and how I will array the planes/crew in there. I had purchased some S2Fs from L’Arsenal with folded wings. The detail is amazing, but these had two issues: the print supports are very tricky to get out and some are molded into the S2F itself, and the wings are the rounded wings of the later S2Fs, which were not the ones on Hornet at this time. Though I can sand down the wingtips, the supports are a real hassle, so I went searching and found STL files for a nicely detailed S2F online. The only issue here is that the wings were not folded and the MAD boom and tailhook are extended. Since I have the STL files, though, I was able to modify the wings and get them folded. The designer also included a searchlight on the port wing, which is incorrect, so I removed that. But now, I can print as many as I need and fill the hangar deck and flight deck.

I worked on the new Model Monkey Yorktown island today. I trimmed off the SPS-8 mounting platform on the top centerline and added the one I 3D printed on the top port side of the island. The Yorktown island is to the left in the photos. I added the safety netting to my print to avoid delicate fiddly PE work. The Hornet island from 1969 is alongside for comparison. No big box on the front of the island–correct for 1959 Hornet–and also note that the starboard bridge is much more enclosed on 1969 Hornet than it was in 1959, with the Yorktown again being correct. Flag bags are correct on Yorktown for 1959 Hornet as well, and I only have to add some wiring and piping, along with 4 storage lockers on the starboard side, and I should have a very accurate representation of the 1959 Hornet’s island.

I’m starting to think about painting the flight deck. Given that it was wood, the color appears to me more like a stain than a pure deck gray over non-skid. This photo is my best reference. Note that the bow cap is the same color as the hull, superstructure and island, which gives me a point of delineation when settling on a color. My current thinking is Mr. Color 603 for the main flight deck and 601 for the landing area, which looks ever so slightly darker. These are listed as IJN Colors, Maizuru and Kure respectively. My Colourcoats Deck Gray and Flight Deck Gray are both far too dark for this application, and I’m a big fan of Mr. Color combined with Mr. Leveling thinner.
